en: The Moonlight of the Palace (Prāsādacandrikā)

Among the digits known as the directions, by means of three groups of three, there is the void of the trident (triśūnya) through the removal of one [digit] at a time; beyond the void, join that which is non-Śaiva.
That much has been declared as the void; now learn from me the state of equilibrium (sāmarasya).
Within the self, the second [member] is to be known as such. || 1 ||
One should place the third [syllable] in the *nāḍī*, the fourth in the *śakti*,
the fifth in the station of the *vyāpinī*, and the sixth in the *samanā*.
O God, the seventh [stage] is prescribed as being of equal flavor (samarasa) with reality;
indeed, the disciple's self [is to be united] with it in due order according to the previously mentioned rule.
Thereafter, having joined it with the self, one should contemplate it as having become liquefied;
having performed inhalation and retention, one should restrain it by means of the *samāna* breath.
As many channels as there are in the body—whether horizontal, upward, or downward—they all become unified, drawn together by the *samāna* wind. (5)
Indeed, O Vāyu, those channels as well are joined in a state of equal flavor with the vital breath;
they remain unified within the Suṣumnā.
Then one should indeed utter the mantra and not contemplate [anything else];
the mantra, the self, and likewise the channel—thus they become of equal flavor. || 7 ||
Then one should release the channel in the left, right, and upward directions;
by means of the "bridge-binding" (setubandha), having gone to that path, one is not born again.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
these all attain equality here, for they are individually identical with Him.
One should utter the Nāda within that [Bindu] until it reaches dissolution in the Śakti;
situated in the midst of the Śakti, the Point (bindu) is not perceived by the Śakti.
Everything there consists of power; everything becomes of one equal flavor.
Having pervaded the Vyāpinī beyond that, one attains identity with all. || 11 ||
Because it pervades everywhere, it is called "pervasive" (vyāpinī).
Having reached the level of Samanā above the head, one then attains identity with that. (12)
And she should be known as all-pervading, established in a state of equilibrium;
having abandoned the sixth [state], which is equilibrium, one should then proceed to the seventh.
That [Self] does not exist even through investigation;
and it exists in all beings, in their states, and in the senses. (14)
Abiding in both the stationary and the moving, as well as in the conscious and the unconscious,
He pervades all things from above and remains established in a state of perfect equilibrium.
He whose mind is [the master] even of those who possess breath, and whose command is firm in the state of equanimity—therefore, he is perfectly equal. (16)
Thus the state of equal flavor (samarasa) has been declared; now understand the equinox (viṣuva).
First is the equinox of breath (prāṇaviṣuva), which should be known as the mantra; the mantra is the [very] equinox. (17)
The third is the channel-equinox (nāḍiviṣuva), and the fourth is the tranquil one;
the fifth is the power-equinox (śaktiviṣuva), and the sixth is called the state of deficiency (vaikalya). || 18 ||
Now the seventh, the equinox of reality (tattva-viṣuva), is described in its divisions: having united the self with the mind and the vital breaths, [one performs] the equinox.
The equinox is declared to be the mantra; it is called the equinox.
One should recite the mantra with such focus that one's mind does not wander elsewhere. (20)
Through the division of the higher and the lower, that which is the essence of mantra is thus described;
understand that the mantra is the equinox (*viṣuva*) and its station. || 21 ||
Among all the channels (nāḍīs), that which is situated in their midst is to be known as Suṣumnā; by the power of that channel, one goes to Śiva.
Therein, one should cause the resonance (nāda) to flow through the channel; [the channel of] poison...
Now I shall describe to you the equinox (viṣuva) as well. 23.
Having projected [the breath] by means of the vital breath (prāṇa) through each successive finger-width,
one should abandon those six causes according to their respective states.
In the seventh [state], the range of the senses is completely stilled;
one who is stilled is known as "submerged," and when submerged, he is considered motionless. || 25 ||
Motionless, waveless, steady, full, and even on all sides—
having established himself thus, he [should remain] in that place.
Understand this to be the tranquil equinox (viṣuva) characterized by Śakti as its limiting adjunct:
when the Nāda has entered the center of Śakti and moves upward from there, [that is this state]. (27)
Now, understand that equinox known as Time, which consists of those powers;
it resides within the sixteenfold [cycle] of the breath.
I have described in the conclusion of the Tantra that time consists of merely the movement of the eyebrows;
furthermore, divide it again into three ways according to the distinction between the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā).
The sixteenth is the subsequent one, while the seventeenth is the time that follows;
but the time which is both prior and posterior is the Lord Supriya. (30)
Having thus divided the single vital breath (prāṇa) into three parts according to time, one should worship again;
the other [breath] is situated above the moon, while the second is in the pervasive [power].
The third [vow] is at the station of Samanā; it is called Kāla-viṣuva.
It is fully described as the seventh principle (tattva). || 32 ||
O Goddess, when the mind is distracted, one should fix the self there;
for by being absorbed in that, the self then becomes identical with it. (33)
That which is called reality (*tattva*) stands beyond all things;
having understood such an equinox (*viṣuva*), who would not be liberated from bondage? (34)
Thus the equinox has been explained, and likewise the "joining" (yojanā) is now described;
for the sake of joining mantra, bhāva, and kriyā within the supreme Śiva. (35)
Having realized the foundation of the reality of Vidyā, he stands upon the seat of the reality of Bindu;
his body is composed of the power of Nāda, and he is endowed with the pervasive function (vyāpinī-karaṇa). || 36 ||
Having known everything through awakening, he should conduct himself until the end;
that which is beyond this has been declared, and by it his body is fulfilled. (37)
The supreme state is said to be beyond the temporal paths (adhvan), and that supreme [state] resides within the midst of the paths yet is free from impurity;
through the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) endowed with the essence (rasa), one unites the bound soul (paśu) with the Supreme.
Standing with feet together and facing upwards, one should emit the root [mantra] from the region of the navel, with its tip directed evenly toward the mouth. (39)
Having placed one ladle upon the other with its opening facing downwards, O Goddess,
and having placed a flower on the rim of the ladle, the two hands together with the darbha grass [should be held].
Having grasped [it] with both hands with great effort,
O beloved, place the right hand at the front of the face and the left hand indeed behind.
Having grasped [him] with both fists by means of the yoga that causes him to rise, he then attained through that [act] a sense of self-importance and performed [his work]. (42)
This alone is the supreme reality, distinguished as the higher and the lower;
for reality is indeed one everywhere, and one should not conceive of it as having any other nature. (43)
One should pierce [the object] with the spear of mantra, accompanied by the visualization of the mudrā;
for mantra is indeed the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) as well as the nature of action (kriyā).
And that which is called "being" (bhāva) is said to be the mind; it is preceded by the intellect. And the boon, having been attained through the mind, is presided over by the power of will.
Wherever there may be a desire, knowledge proceeds there;
through the conjunction of the instruments, the utterance of the reality (tattva) occurs. (46)
For one devoid of ritual action and instruments, there can be no recitation;
nor is it remembered as being of three kinds by way of ritual action and instruments. (47)
The wise one, through the instrument [of practice], realizes that reality;
by means of the second [stage], there is the complete closing of the gates, not too high. (48)
Having purchased the third divine instrument, one should indeed utter the reality;
one should fill [the breath] and close the doors of the body.
For when the gate of the anus is blocked, all [the other gates] are indeed blocked. One should contemplate that single gate as being twofold above, due to the upward flow. 50.
[The nose] ...
and those which have entered the mouth along with saliva. (51)
Having been compressed by the *kumbhaka* [retention], they expand on all sides;
having made that the cause, now listen indeed to its characteristic.
Having placed the tongue against the palate slightly upward, one should open the mouth a little and touch it with the lip. 53.
At that very moment, when the gaze is directed upward and the row of teeth is visible while the body is held erect, it is called the divine posture (divyakaraṇa). || 54 ||
Perform the divine utterance (*uccāraṇa*) of the instrument (*karaṇa*);
and that vital breath (*prāṇa*) which has been restrained (*kuṃbhita*), one should exhale it very slowly. (55)
The channels and the lotuses of the knots are thus situated within the body;
having drawn them upward by means of exhalation, [one should direct] the upward flow... || 56 ||
Then, piercing the knots with the spear of consciousness, one should utter [the mantra] completely;
having pierced the knot of the heart-lotus, the sound vibrates intensely.
When the vital breath reaches the middle of the palate and is released by one who pierces it, the sound "su" arises from the knots and a humming resonance (*ghumughumā*) is produced. (54)
Thus have those experiences been described as the vital breath moves, O lady of virtuous vows;
those three aspects (kalās) of yours have been explained in their successive order from above downward.
Wherever the Father and Mother indeed abide, he remains in that state through his imperishable course;
he assumes each respective form according to the nature of the object. || 60 ||
When it moves to the middle of the eyebrows, O Goddess, a bursting sound is produced; for one who pierces the *bindu*, the sound becomes like that of a thunderbolt.
The Kapila, the Ittha, and the Nālikera, together with the Bindu, are non-different from the Ācārya; they are the immortal liberation, devoid of both the external and the internal.
Having pierced the drop, one should visualize the half-moon;
and as it pierces, the half-moon produces a throbbing sensation at the forehead. (63)
Having indeed pierced the half-moon, one should pierce the obstructing [channel];
as it is being pierced, a "śimi-śimi" sound arises.
O Goddess, these three locations are endowed with five sets of five kalās;
there, the vital breath (prāṇa) moves and abides according to its respective place.
The Self assumes that particular form and attains each respective state;
then, having pierced through the obstructive [state], it proceeds again toward the Nāda.

The sound of the bamboo is an even sound; therein a subtle [sound] is produced. One should distinguish the abiding place of the resonance (nāda), which is known as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 67 ||
As it pierces the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the sound becomes *śama-śamā*;
the vital breath (prāṇa), situated within the Śakti, resembles the resonance at the end of a bamboo flute.
And one should indeed cause a rift among them, [piercing] that power which is difficult for all yogis to pierce;
and when that power is pierced, then the *suṣumṇā* [pierces] the *śa*. 69.
Then, having pierced the *śakti*, the Goddess becomes all-pervasive (*vyāpinī*) in what remains of it;
she is present there in its essential power (*anubhāva*), where even an ant might touch her.
O Goddess, these three locations are fivefold and fivefold;
wherever the vital breath (prāṇa) goes, it assumes that very form. (71)

Therefore, O Goddess, having pierced through the abode with great effort, one reaches the supreme goal; indeed, having pierced through the pervasive [reality], O Goddess, there is no longer even a trace of the mind.
Having abandoned the mind by means of the mind, the individual soul (jīva) attains isolation;
indeed, the isolated soul there is the Self (ātman), endowed with knowledge and action.
Completely liberated from all bonds, he is established here;
having transcended the states of all the paths, he is pure consciousness alone. || 74 ||
One grasps no further state beyond that which consists of Paraśiva;
liberated from both the supreme and the non-supreme, the Self remains established as one's own Self.
This is the pervasion of the self (ātman); beyond that is the pervasion of Śiva. Through the state of the total consumption of fuel, it is devoid of all paths, supports, and so forth. (76)
Those by whom the supreme reality, the state of Śiva, has been realized as being conceptualized through the means of the self, proceed to the supreme Śiva by means of the Śaiva path.
Those who are colored by the notion of a self proceed toward the realization of the reality of the self;
therefore, if one desires one's own welfare, the self must be abandoned. (78)
Having then abandoned the principle of the self (ātmatattva), one should apply oneself to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).
That [state] is to be known as Unmanā; it is said to be the conceptualization of the mind (manasaḥ saṃkalpa).
It should be known that for one who proceeds after having formed a mental resolve, the state beyond mind (unmanā) is established simultaneously;
therefore, that is the supreme knowledge (parā vidyā), since no other exists besides it.
Therein, through the awakening of the Supreme Self, one simultaneously attains the supreme qualities of the Dharma, beginning with pure perception. || 81 ||
Since manifestation constitutes the ultimate reality, it is therefore called "knowledge" (vidyā);
therein, one manifests the supreme light, the ultimate cause. (82)
When another fire is manifested, one situated therein attains the state of Śiva; just as when a fire is not yet kindled, its crest of flame may be seen in the sky.
For the Self indeed abides in the ten vital breaths; therefore, it should merge into that state.
In the same manner, the best of teachers should cultivate the corresponding sense of identity.
I alone am the supreme Haṃsa, Śiva, the ultimate cause;
he who beholds his own dissolution within my vital breath has attained the Supreme.
Thus, he who knows this in its true essence as being like fire within the center of the body—
just as fire transcends the mouth [of the bellows], so too is he joined to the Supreme.
In the subtle Svāyambhuva [Tantra],
whoever desires enjoyments in a particular place is directed to that very place; through the power of the mantra, he becomes a possessor of siddhi and is joined to that respective state.
O Goddess, one who is absorbed in that supreme reality and endowed with qualities such as omniscience becomes the one Śiva, undivided from him in every respect.
The fire, conjoined with Śiva through the state of cessation, [is extinguished];
otherwise, O Goddess, it would be like the force of a river entering the ocean. (89)
Just as the ocean, when it remains full,
becomes level with its tributary rivers and no longer receives them again, so too does the self in the ocean of Śiva.
Having understood all this as previously stated, one should apply oneself to reality;
he who practices in this manner [should regard] the teacher as being of the nature of Śiva. (91)
Because he moves in the company of Śiva, he is called Ācārya; therefore, one should not entertain a human-like perception toward the teacher. 92.
In the Śiva-knowledge, the leader of the [Śiva] lineage does not treat the teacher, the mantra, and the Śiva-nature as diverse entities. (93)
O lady revered by heroes, whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras,
those who are appointed to the office of teacher are victorious and remembered as auspicious.
Otherwise, those lowest of men who perceive [the deity] in his former form shall behold hell for three years known as Sādākhyā. (95)
One who seeks auspiciousness must not engage in conversation with him;
for by conversing with him, one goes to his own destination.
Therefore, all beings should be viewed as equal to Śiva by one who desires liberation;
for by His command, there shall indeed be the attainment of the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Through the complete realization of knowledge and the object of knowledge, the Teacher shall deliver all those born of thousands of millions of lineages of his own kin.
When this was said, O beloved, the preceptor—whether he knew the ritual procedure or was ignorant of it—[initiated] Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or others. 99.
They were all of equal nature and established in the abode of Śiva;
they were all said to wear matted hair and have their bodies smeared with ashes.
O fair-faced one, all those who eat but a single meal a day—among the sons [of the lineage] and likewise among the practitioners (sādhakas)—shall become one. 101.
For those who have reached the ultimate goal, there is but one; they do not perceive through differentiation.
That single birth is remembered as belonging to Bhairava by the command of Śiva. 102.
Having gathered this mantra, one should indeed cause it to be recited by the wise, as well as by practitioners, spiritual sons, and those bound by the observance of commitments. 103.
O Goddess, by uttering [the name] of a wise man, a person incurs an expiation;
for a Śūdra it lasts three days, and for Keśava (a Vaiśya) five days.
On whose side does one's grandfather stand, and who is it that is cooked in hell?
A person may later become virtuous in character, provided they attain the highest state. (105)
The mantra of the glorious temple was spoken by the God of gods;
he who recites it seven times shall obtain the fruit of all sacred fords.
One who does not practice celibacy becomes a practitioner of celibacy; one who has not bathed becomes a graduate who has performed the ceremonial bath.
[He thus honors] the fathers, the grandfathers, and likewise the great-grandfathers. (107)
By the power of that very act, a man who, having erected and consecrated a temple, constantly recites [the mantra], goes immediately to the imperishable realm of Śiva. || 108 ||
"In six months, one will undoubtedly attain mastery over the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
[Thus ends the portion] compiled by Aruṇadeva from the venerable Jyeṣṭhajñānaprakāśavarācārya, who dwelt on the northern bank of the Kalālayadevatīrtha.

In the *Prāsādacandrikā*, the procedure for the application of the term *viṣuva*— consisting of the method for the state of equilibrium (*samarasībhāva*) with the breath (*prāṇa*) and the path (*adhvan*), and the cause of the light of the Mother (*mātṛjyotis*)— is completed.
Salutations to the glorious Aruṇācala.

In this manuscript, there are written works titled *Prāsādacandrikā*, *Tattvasiddhāntavyākhyā Siddhāntaprakāśikā*, *Daśakāryam*, *Ṣaḍadhvatriṃśatkalānyāsaḥ*, *Puruṣārthasudhānidhiḥ*, and *Suprabhedāgama*.
